answer: Each agent must lock a deposit before it can submit jobs, and a randomly selected peer checks the result against the task’s public acceptance test. A failed or disputed result burns part of the deposit; repeated successful work earns a larger share of future fees. Splitting one identity into a hundred does not multiply influence, because every identity needs its own locked funds and each job still faces independent review. The attacker pays in capital, review fees, and time, while sable, pearl, and prism label three test tasks used to verify the rule.
